rationale: History: baseline 128x64x64 s1 t256 sw0=3560.55us; 32x256x32 s1 t256 sw64=3518.99us; 32x256x32 s1 t128 sw64=2504.88us (best, 330MB DRAM, 3 blocks/SM); 64x128x32 s2 t256 sw64=3989.52us; 32x256x32 s1 t64 sw64=2891.16us (210 regs, worse than t128). Lessons: threads=128 dominates 256 and 64 for the winning wide-N tile (higher occupancy), swizzle=64 with narrow-M/wide-N cuts simulated DRAM roughly in half and correlates with lower latency, and stage=2 with narrow-N or t256 regressed. This plan forces a new structural point rather than revisiting the same 32x256x32 tuple: threads fixed to {128} as the measured winner, swizzle narrowed to {32,64} (both large panels) to test whether panel size beyond 32 matters, block_M kept >=32 (16 was dropped as low-reuse), block_N >=128 retaining wide-N, block_K still spans 32-128, and num_stages narrowed to {1,2} since 3-4 with these small shared-memory budgets have not shown benefit and s2 already regressed at t256. Weights: traffic 2 (DRAM reduction matched latency gains at t128), launches 0.5 (4096^2 grid already large), pipeline 1 (stage benefit unproven), footprint 1 to keep under the 32768 cap via max(2*block_K*(block_M+block_N)*num_stages, 4*block_M*block_N). Next hypothesis: test whether block_K=64/128 at stage>=1 with a wider block_M (64/128) and t128 can beat 2504.88us, and whether swizzle=32 vs 64 differentiates once threads and stage are held; if larger swizzle panels lose, drop them next round. Scope: Metal checks simulate exact source/config/TIR; the CUDA binary is not executed, and all GB10 values are simulator estimates, not hardware measurements; no global optimality is claimed.
